channel_name: The Prof G Show · Scott Galloway
video_title: David Brooks: Trump Gutted Conservatism and Christianity
gist: Midterm-week rebroadcast of a May 2025 Scott Galloway interview with David Brooks. Brooks argues Trump runs reactionary, anti-left politics rather than conservatism, and says progressive institutions built an education-based caste system that fed the backlash. Both men call for expanding elite university capacity and pressuring endowments, and they trace US political dysfunction to a breakdown of social and moral fabric. Little market content; the investor-relevant signal is on higher-education policy risk, where Biden-era industrial spending landed, and the politics of class and respect.

insights.claim: David Brooks splits the American right into 'pro-conservatives' (John McCain, Mitt Romney, George W. Bush) and the 'anti-left' (the Dartmouth Review circle, including Laura Ingraham and Dinesh D'Souza, plus Peter Thiel and Vivek Ramaswamy). He says the anti-left faction now dominates and that Trump practices reactionary politics, not conservatism.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: This lens helps read GOP factional power: the Thiel/Ramaswamy-style anti-establishment wing, rather than institutional conservatives, drives policy direction.
insights.quote: whatever conservatism is, it is definitely not what Trump does. He creates reactionary politics, something completely different.

insights.claim: Brooks argues that Trump's open pursuit of worldly power and dominance has hollowed out ('emasculated') both conservatism and Christianity, the two belief systems Trump claims to champion.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Elite center-right commentators are breaking with the GOP on values, which may erode support among educated suburban and religious voters.
insights.quote: Donald Trump is completely focused on secular power. It's about dominance.

insights.claim: Brooks describes his political ideal as Hamiltonianism: limited but energetic government aimed at social mobility. He contrasts it with progressives, who use government to advance equality, and libertarians, who limit government to expand freedom.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It marks the space for a pro-industrial-policy, pro-mobility centrism that differs from both libertarian and progressive economics.
insights.quote: Hamiltonianism believes in limited but energetic government to increase social mobility.

insights.claim: Brooks says the day the Trump tariffs were announced gave him a new feeling of patriotic shame, combined with what he called 'the horror of incompetence'. He had felt that shame earlier when Trump attacked Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It shows that center-right opinion leaders saw the tariff rollout as incompetent rather than strategic, a signal of how much elite credibility the trade policy has.
insights.quote: on the day of the layoffs, when the tariffs were announced, I felt it again, combined with the horror of incompetence.

insights.claim: Brooks, a lifelong conservative who worked at National Review, the Wall Street Journal editorial page and The Weekly Standard, now places himself with moderates and Democrats. Quoting Isaiah Berlin, he says he is on 'the right edge of the left'.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It is a personal example of the realignment of college-educated center-right voters toward Democrats.
insights.quote: I'm happy to be on the right edge of the left.

insights.claim: Scott Galloway argues that Democrats' habit of going too far set up the backlash. His examples are about 250,000 border crossings in December 2023 and campus DEI bureaucracies that grew so large they 'probably unknowingly and accidentally became racist'.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Even left-leaning commentators accept the overreach story, which suggests Democrats will move toward the center on immigration and DEI.
insights.quote: We allowed 250,000 people to cross the border in December 2023, which caused a backlash

insights.claim: Brooks calls progressives' biggest sin of the past 70 years the creation of universities, media, cultural institutions and nonprofits with no room for working-class or conservative views. He claims no Trump supporter holds an editorial position at any major media outlet.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It explains the durable distrust of legacy media and institutions on the right, and the opening for alternative media platforms.
insights.quote: there is not a single Trump supporter in an editorial position

insights.claim: Galloway says campus DEI bureaucracies should be dismantled, pointing out that 60% of Harvard freshmen identify as non-white and questioning what a 140-person DEI apparatus actually does.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: A prominent left-of-center voice backing DEI cuts points to bipartisan room for university administrative downsizing.

insights.claim: Brooks argues that universities that cast themselves as the activist wing of the Democratic Party invited the Republican attacks they now face. He hopes the pressure from Trump will push them back toward a humanistic, character-building and civic mission.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Political pressure on higher education looks structural, not a passing episode, which matters for university funding, endowments and education-sector exposure.
insights.quote: if you tie your university to a political party and say that you're activists

insights.claim: Brooks cites education-gap data. Americans with higher education live 15 years longer than those with only secondary education. Those with only a high school education are five times more likely to die of opioid addiction and five times more likely to have children out of wedlock. They are also 2.4 times more likely to say they have no friends.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Educational attainment is the main fault line driving US health, social and political outcomes, with implications for healthcare demand and voting.
insights.quote: People with higher education live 15 years longer than people with secondary education.

insights.claim: Brooks cites a study finding that 54% of workers in media, entertainment, law and science graduated from the same 32 elite colleges. He adds that banks and consulting firms recruit at only a few select schools.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Elite-pipeline hiring is concentrated, which sustains the pricing power of elite schools and the political resentment against them.
insights.quote: 54% of workers in these fields graduated from the same 32 elite colleges.

insights.claim: Brooks says elite schools such as Harvard send glossy recruiting brochures to students who will mostly be rejected, inflating applications so they can advertise rejecting 96% of applicants. He calls this deliberate artificial scarcity.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Selectivity is a marketing metric that schools optimize, not a reflection of capacity limits, which strengthens the case for regulators to push expansion.
insights.quote: we reject 96% of the children who apply to our school

insights.claim: Galloway proposes stripping tax-exempt status from universities with endowments over $1 billion that don't grow freshman enrollment as fast as the population.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: This kind of endowment-tax or enrollment-mandate proposal is a policy risk for large endowments and the asset managers and allocators that serve them.
insights.quote: you're no longer a government institution, you're a hedge fund with tuition.

insights.claim: Galloway argues that the fight over admissions criteria (analytical versus qualitative metrics, DEI) distracts from the real question of how many students elite schools admit. He notes that lower-tier colleges with open access have no comparable DEI conflicts.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: It recasts higher-ed reform around capacity, which favors expansion and online or scaled education models over fights about allocation.

insights.claim: Selectivity has risen sharply. Galloway says UCLA's acceptance rate fell from 76% to 9%, and the University of Chicago now admits about 4%, compared with roughly 74% when Brooks attended.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway / David Brooks
insights.so_what: Elite seat supply is fixed while demand grows, showing the scarcity rents that elite institutions capture.

insights.claim: Galloway compares American gatekeeping to LVMH-style exclusivity. Once people own a home, their incentive is to block new building so its value rises, and the same pull-up-the-ladder dynamic runs through elite institutions.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Incumbent-driven artificial scarcity in housing and education explains persistent supply constraints and the price inflation in both.

insights.claim: Brooks argues that meritocracy has narrowly defined ability since the 1930s-1950s as IQ, test scores and pleasing teachers at ages 15-18, which wealthy parents can easily game. A broader definition that includes curiosity, drive and social skills would be spread more evenly across the population.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It points to the possible erosion of standardized testing as a gatekeeper and to demand for alternative talent assessment.
insights.quote: This entire system is based on defining aptitude as the ability to flatter teachers between the ages of 15 and 18 and to do well on standardized tests.

insights.claim: Brooks sees US universities as having moved through five regimes: piety, humanism, research, careerism, and then social justice, which filled the moral void left by the last two. He wants a return to humanistic and civic ideals.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: This is a model for how universities may reposition their missions under political pressure.

insights.claim: Galloway says many university courses on sustainability, leadership and ethics, including some at his own school, mostly generate student debt and give speaking slots to 'former important people'.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: An insider is skeptical of the value of soft-skill degrees, which supports pressure on the tuition ROI of non-core programs.

insights.claim: Brooks says most of the money from Build Back Better and the big Biden infrastructure bills went to rural Republican districts. He cites a map by Rahm Emanuel, then US ambassador to Japan, showing that only two of the first hundred big chip-plant and industrial investments were in California, while Illinois, Iowa and upstate New York each had five to seven.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Because industrial-policy capex sits mostly in red districts, the projects have bipartisan local constituencies that make repeal politically hard.
insights.quote: out of the first hundred, only two were in California

insights.claim: Brooks names Intel's plant in eastern Ohio and Micron's plant near Syracuse as visible local examples of economic revival from the industrial-investment wave. He says the revival had not blossomed enough to reward Biden politically.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Semiconductor fab projects take years to pay off economically and politically, so the payoff lags the election cycle.

insights.claim: Brooks argues Biden's second mistake was assuming economic resources alone could repair working-class alienation. Left-behind places lost status and respect as well as material standing, and he calls bridging that cultural gap the Democrats' main challenge.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Fiscal transfers do not reliably buy votes, which tempers forecasts that rest on industrial-policy spending to shift elections.
insights.quote: It's not just that these places have been left behind materially, they have been left behind in terms of status and respect.

insights.claim: Brooks cites two figures on social collapse: 45% of teenagers say they constantly feel hopeless and despairing, and the number of Americans with no close friends has quadrupled since 2000. He calls this spiritual and interpersonal crisis the deep root cause of US political dysfunction.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Loneliness and mental-health deterioration is a long-running driver of demand for mental-health, community and social products, and of political volatility.
insights.quote: The number of Americans who say they have no close friends has quadrupled since 2000.

insights.claim: Brooks argues that capitalism needs an opposing moral system, such as Catholicism, Judaism, progressivism or environmentalism, to check its worst flaws. He says all of these counterweights are collapsing, leaving money as the dominant ethos.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Weaker moral counterweights to profit-seeking may add to populist backlash and regulatory risk for businesses seen as purely extractive.

insights.claim: Brooks says that after World War II, institutions from schools to the Girl Scouts dropped moral education for self-actualization and careerism, built on the belief that people are inherently good. He links that loss directly to a country that saw nothing wrong with electing Donald Trump.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: This long-cycle cultural diagnosis suggests political polarization will not quickly reverse with election outcomes.

insights.claim: Brooks strongly backs mandatory national service as a way to mix classes and regions (for example, young people from Berkeley meeting young people from Birmingham, Alabama) and to give twenty-somethings a sense of purpose.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Bipartisan elite interest in national service could eventually affect youth labor supply and education pathways.

insights.claim: Brooks's response to the social-fabric crisis is Weave: The Social Fabric Project, a nonprofit that funds and promotes local community trust-builders. His theory is that culture changes when a small group finds a better way of life and others copy it.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Philanthropy for community-rebuilding is growing as a response to loneliness.
insights.quote: culture changes when a small group of people find a better way of life and the rest of us follow suit.

insights.claim: Brooks credits Richard Reeves with showing that the crisis of men and boys is not zero-sum with women's progress. He argues the core driver is a loss of meaning and of outlets for 'energetic virtues' (courage, risk-taking, strength), which explains the appeal of muscular, discipline-focused podcasters to young men.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: Young men's unmet demand for challenge and self-improvement explains the reach of fitness and discipline media and the 'manosphere'.

insights.claim: Galloway says about 80% of the Prof G podcast's audience is male, and that Brooks's 2022 New York Times column 'The Crisis of Men and Boys' led him to Richard Reeves and to making the issue his focus.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: It shows how male-skewed the business and finance podcast audience is.

insights.claim: Brooks argues that overprotective parenting has sharply limited young people's opportunities for adventure, which boys and girls both want.
insights.speaker: David Brooks
insights.so_what: It points to demand for structured adventure and outdoor experiences for young people.
